source: Father... I know that you have, in your possession, the journals of King Hamlet. Can I see them?
I have the—what?
How could you know...?
Never mind that. I need to see them, father. Please—it's urgent.
They're stored and locked in my personal chest, Ophelia. I find it eerie that you would know of such a thing.
They've been destroyed. The ashes are still warm, in fact.
I saw to it last night that such documents can cause no harm.
I saw to it two nights past that such documents can cause us no harm.
I saw to it three nights past that such documents can cause us no harm.
The things they discuss... they could tarnish the reputation of the King forever, brand him a lunatic. I can't have that, not with the court in such a delicate state.
(So... I'm too late. He's gone and burned them.)
(If he burned them Thursday evening... perhaps there's a way I can stop him.)
(I've missed my chance to salvage those notes in this world.)
I don't know how you learned about them, but they are best left unread, with the court in such a delicate state.
I thought no one but I knew of their existence. If that's not true... then I have some unfinished business to attend to.
Father, please, don't. Hand them to me.
Leave me be, now. For your own good.
I've been told my father might have some notes which were written by the late King Hamlet.
Ah, mysteries upon mysteries upon mysteries...
I would hate to think of the stir those might raise!
Of course, they might also be soggy love poems. Harmless and simple.
Who knows!
Of course. You already know what they contain, don't you?
Look at you! Spreading dangerous information just to see what happens. There may be hope for you yet.
We're closing in on the end of the game, now. Just a few more threads to unravel.
You say my father has your personal journals. If so, where are they?
There are gaps in my knowledge between my death and my... awakening.
I know not where they live now. Only that he has certainly taken them from where they once lay.
Your brother was apparently searching for a strange old book before his death. Do you know anything about it?
Not in the slightest. What sort of a book? My brother always was the learned sort... Myself, I'm partial to the sword.
I'm not certain what it might look like. But he was... obsessed with finding it. Did he ever do anything strange to that extent?
It's a little brown book with gold trim. He was obsessed with finding it. Did he ever do anything strange to that extent?
I see. Yes, there was something like that.
In the days leading up to his death, he spent every waking moment in the gallery, poring over every page he could find.
It was as though he was consumed by something. Any time I spoke to him, it was as though he couldn't see me. Or he seemed frustrated that I'd disrupted him.
I'd encourage you to have a look through the collection, but many of those books are a bit too stimulating for a young woman's mind.
Mind your health first.
My lady, your late husband was searching for a strange old book before his death. Surely you know of it.
What sort of book do you mean?
I'm not certain what it might look like. But he was... obsessed with finding it.
It's a little dark book with gold trim. He was obsessed with finding it.
I don't know anything about a book in particular, but it's true that in the week before he passed, my husband took frequent trips into town.
He never did tell me what he was searching for, mind you. But your father always accompanied him, ever faithful.
I suppose I shall never know what consumed him, rest his soul.
Much though I might wish I did.
I've learned that your father may have come across a strange book. Do you know anything about it?
You mean... the one he mentioned in... those notes.
I don't know. He never told me about anything like that. Or about... anything else he wrote.
I want to forget what I saw. But I can't. He was—completely and totally insane.
And now I'm going to be like that too, aren't I? My father, and me, and my grandmother, too.
Astrid. She died long before I was born. But they say insanity runs in our blood. And now I know it must be true.
(Hmm. That's a connection worth exploring.)
You mean Astrid.
Yes. She died long before I was born. But they say that because of her, insanity runs in our blood.
Perhaps I was doomed a long time ago.
He loved reading. Do you expect I tracked every tome in his library?
No—it wasn't a book he owned. It was something he was searching for. Something special.
What might it look like?
I've no idea.
Then what can you expect from me? Of course I don't know how to find something with no description.
It's a little brown book with gold trim.
There are a hundred books fitting that description in the gallery. I can be of no help with this.
Father, I know the King was searching for a strange book before he died. Do you know where to find it?
How... how did you hear about that?
Never mind that. I'd like to find out where that book went. What do you know?
I don't know about any such book, Ophelia. And whatsoever you were told, whenever King Hamlet and I went into town together, I saw nothing of his activities!
Wait, Father. Into town? What activities can you mean?
The King would often ask me to accompany him into town while he spoke to, shall we say, odd acquaintances. But I neither had any direct hand in it, nor overheard a word.
So, perhaps if I were to visit town...
Don't even think about it, dearheart. A terrible port town filled with thieves and vagrants. It's not for you.
Regardless, only the King himself knows what he was searching for in town. So it's lost to time forever, I expect. Better not to dally in it.
About this cursed book...
Oh, dear, yes. That book is the source of all sorrow, all chaos.
And now you're bound to me until you hand it over.
You can give it to me any time you like.
I politely decline.
But what is it about the book's power that you so desire?
I don't know that I can impart it upon you, really.
It would be like trying to explain the fearsome quality of fire to a dust mote.
The only way to do so would be to show you.
Perhaps someday, when you've used the Book's power enough, you'll be ready for me to show you something special.
But today is not that day.
I gave you the power to find out for yourself, Ophelia.
Stop being a coward and explore what that power has to offer.
I had it under my control, once. But it's been lost.
And so your fate and mine are tied, as well as that miserable spirit's.
So you know of it? And you never told me?
Would you have believed me?
Likely not.
If you find it, bring it to me immediately, lest it cause any more pain and loss.
As you've now realized, it's far too dangerous to occupy human hands.
I have every intention of destroying it immediately, as someone ought to have done long ago.
...You haven't attended my little play about this very matter, have you?
Why, I must say, it truly is my magnum opus, if I do say so myself.
Castle Town! Thursday morning! You'll be my guest of honor!
(That's before he's come to Elsinore. All right, I'll find him then.)
I found your notes. They mentioned you were looking for a 'cursed book'.
You were... trapped, weren't you? Just like I am now.
I can feel the cobwebs of my memory being dusted away gently.
Ah, to be alive, to remember... my utter failure.
That book... I gave up in the end, didn't I? And I let... that cursed thing win, break me down...
You mean the book?
Please. I know it's confusing, but start at the beginning, if you can. What happened?
Yes. Like you, I was doomed to repeat the occasion of my death. Hundreds of times. Thousands.
And like you, the timeline of my death was no more than a week. My son Hamlet was away at Wittenberg, my brother Claudius plotting to take my throne.
How long was I trapped in that insane void between life and death? Centuries? Millennia? I know not...
It was peaceful to forget for a while, but even now, I cannot be truly dead. No, here I am, still animated, grimacing, like a starved dog brought back to life, forced to bare my teeth...
I cannot truly rest until my brother pays for his crime, the crime I spent a thousand years trying to avoid!
Why were you looking for the book? What did you expect to find?
A way out!
A choice between versions of a private hell!
But I was not permitted that much! No, I had to give up! I lay there in the garden, being poisoned by my own brother over and over again, for years before I was freed!
I scoured every inch of the castle, every nook and flagstone and drawer—it isn't here, Ophelia! It simply isn't!
Why did I have to give up, to expire into madness alone?
I'm sorry, King Hamlet. I wish I could have found the book long ago, for your sake.
(But now that I have it, I have to decide what to do with it.)
(...And figure out what to do about Quince.)
Ophelia! Find the book! Find the book and save your own soul!
I know about Simona. I know she hid it intentionally, took it with her.
You know that name? How? How can you know?
...I'm going to put you to rest, King Hamlet. I've decided.
I'll find her and get the book from her. I'll end this for both of us. I swear.
It is eternally more worthwhile to fight than to give up as I did, Ophelia. Never forget that. For you, hope lingers.
I believe that you will live to see winter come to Denmark—putting an end to this cursed summer.
(So much is riding on me now.)
(I've got to find a way to get that damned book.)
I'm doing my best, but I don't know where to begin looking.
Perhaps it is too late, after all.
Insanity—death—they have always plagued our family. My mother Astrid was no exception.
I often wonder if she died like me, if she saw time repeating itself. I cannot bear to think of her suffering the same pain I did.
If she was, do you think she might have had something to do with this book's disappearance?
If it's the only thing which can break us free—then mightn't she have found it?
Impossible to tell. My mother is long dead.
